items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: But Teddy Wilson, he had a style which was simple but beautiful, you know?

ctx.x: Well there’s a number of people along the way who wanted your sound, that’s for sure.
Well I’ve, in my era, there was so much competition. It was very competitive in New York at that time. And Charlie Shavers, and so many good trumpet players and they all © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

had their own style. They had their own sound. There was no doubt when you heard them playing you could be ten miles away and hear them play and say, “that’s Charlie Shavers—that’s Dizzy—that’s Louis Armstrong—that’s Red Allen.” Bunny Berigan had a good sound of his own. But Teddy Wilson, he had a style which was simple but beautiful, you know?

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: A lot of people for a long time would put down the later recordings and say that the ones from the ‘30’s with Teddy Wilson were really the epitome of her accomplishment. How would you assess the two periods in which you worked with her?

ctx.x: Yeah. And Teddy Wilson, he introduced me to Teddy Wilson. Well, Basie had a popular band anyway and everybody loved him because he was just down-to-earth guy. He would be hanging out in New York, maybe he’d go to sleep in his car on 126th Street, we’d be playing at the Apollo and nobody would bother him, say, oh that’s Count, look after him. He’d shoot craps with the guys on 126th Street, everybody loved him.
What was his role as a leader, it sounds like he was one of the guys. Could he discipline the band if necessary?

items.title: 66600_Teddy Wilson oral history interview
items.q: I'll tell you who turns that kind of stuff on nowadays is Harry Edison. You ever see Harry Edison tangle up with musicians, they get kidding around, ride each other.

Yeah, 'Seen better days on a farm,' he used to say, something like that. Yeah, Sweets is quite a character and a fantastic player.

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: Teddy Wilson spent a lot of time in Ohio with Speed Webb... McKinney's Cotton Pickers came through there. They had Roy Eldridge, Billy Bowen, Teddy Wilson...

ctx.x: Yes, I know that. I was wondering why -- you know, I always thought of Crawford as playing in Memphis but I knew Sy came from up there.

He's from Zanesville. And the Mills Brothers are from Pickaway, Ohio. They're from Ohio. Earl Warren is from Ohio. Teddy Wilson spent a lot of time in Ohio with Speed Webb, he was from Ohio. Chick Carter, Snooky Young's old boss, he's from Ohio. Art Tatum was from Toledo. There are many, many good musicians from Ohio. Eli Robertson, the trombone player, he was from around Ohio.
But see, all those bands used to station themselves in Ohio, Columbus, because they could go to Cincinnati, only 90 miles, go to Steubenville, only 60 miles.
